draft.title: Filtration and decanting
card: a way to separate an undissolved solid from a liquid. The mixture is poured through filter paper, which has tiny holes. The liquid passes through and the solid particles are caught.
The liquid that passes through is the filtrate. The solid left on the paper is the residue.
a way to pour a liquid off a solid that has settled to the bottom. The solid stays in the container.
Both methods separate an undissolved solid from a liquid. A dissolved solid is spread out as tiny particles in the liquid, so it is not caught by filter paper.
draft.remember: Filtration catches solids in paper. Decanting pours liquid off settled solid.

a.q: Sand and water are poured through filter paper in a funnel. What is left on the filter paper?
a.why: The sand is an undissolved solid, so the holes in the paper are too small for it to pass. It stays on the paper as the residue. The water that passes through is the filtrate, so the option with water as the filtrate has the wrong substance on the paper.
a.clue: Which part of the mixture is too big to pass through the holes?

b.q: Ravi stirs salt into a jug of water until it disappears. He then pours the jug through filter paper. What is most likely to happen?
opts: The salt water passes through and no salt is caught
The salt is caught on the paper as the residue
The water is caught and only the salt passes through
The salt settles so Ravi can decant the water off
b.why: The salt has dissolved, so it is spread through the water as tiny particles that pass through the holes in the paper. Nothing is caught. Filtering only catches undissolved solid, so the option about salt left as residue is wrong.
b.clue: Has the salt dissolved or is it still an undissolved solid?

b.best: The salt water passes through and no salt is caught

check.summary: No problems found. Both questions have one clear right answer that matches the card, and the explanations agree with it.
